items.stem: What problem do actors solve in Swift concurrency?

options.text: They serialise access to their mutable state, preventing data races
options.rationale: Actor isolation ensures only one task touches the actor's state at a time.

options.text: They make synchronous code run faster
options.rationale: Actors are about safe state access, not raw speed.

options.text: They replace all need for async/await
options.rationale: Actors are used together with async/await.

options.text: They guarantee UI code runs off the main thread
options.rationale: MainActor specifically pins work to the main thread.

items.explanation: Actor isolation ensures only one task touches the actor's state at a time.

items.stem: Select TWO correct distinctions between some and any for a protocol P in Swift.

options.text: some P is an opaque type: one concrete underlying type fixed at compile time
options.rationale: Opaque types hide but fix a single concrete type.

options.text: any P is an existential that can hold different conforming types at runtime
options.rationale: Existentials box any conformer and can vary dynamically.

options.text: some P can hold a different concrete type on each call
options.rationale: The underlying type is fixed per return position.

options.text: any P is resolved entirely at compile time with no boxing

items.explanation: Opaque types hide but fix a single concrete type.

items.stem: Why can copy-on-write make Swift arrays efficient despite value semantics?

options.text: The underlying buffer is shared until a mutation forces a unique copy
options.rationale: COW defers copying until a write occurs on a shared buffer.
Arrays are value types; COW gives value semantics efficiently.

options.text: Mutations never copy under any circumstances
options.rationale: A mutation of a shared buffer triggers a copy.
COW is unrelated to bounds checking.

items.explanation: COW defers copying until a write occurs on a shared buffer.
